paper_sections.title: Reduced Functional Connectivity within the Mesocorticolimbic System in Substance Use Disorders: An fMRI Study of Puerto Rican Young Adults

description.value: The study examined resting-state functional connectivity of bilateral nucleus accumbens seeds within the mesocorticolimbic system in Puerto Rican young adults with and without substance use disorders, including associations with impulsivity and effects of scan site.

design.value: A cross-sectional, observational resting-state fMRI study compared seed-based mesocorticolimbic connectivity between young adults with and without SUD, tested site moderation, and conducted exploratory partial-correlation and path analyses.

name.value: a large, epidemiological study of Puerto Ricans in the South Bronx, New York and San Juan, Puerto Rico

description.value: T1-weighted sagittal localizing images were acquired, followed by a high-resolution anatomical image for coregistration with axial echoplanar images.

Standard image preprocessing methods were used, employing SPM8 Software with the conn_toolbox for functional connectivity analysis. Connectivity preprocessing procedures followed the component-based noise correction method to minimize non-neural influences on fMRI signal.

steps.value: Coregistration with a high-resolution anatomical scan
Normalization into Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space
Smoothing with a Gaussian kernel of 6 mm 3 full width at half maximum (FWHM)
Voxel-by-voxel correlation across the complete resting-time series

model_settings.value: Resting-state fMRI time series data were correlated voxel by voxel for each participant across the complete resting-time series, using bilateral NAcc seed regions; Fisher z transformation was applied.

Seed-based connectivity maps were entered with Group as the single factor with two levels (SUD+ and SUD−), comorbid disorders as a covariate dummy coded 1 or 0, and motion parameters as nuisance regressors at the subject- and group-level. Group comparisons were anatomically restricted to OFC, amygdala, hippocampus, NAcc, and midbrain/VTA regions derived from WFU_pickatlas; exploratory whole-brain analyses were also conducted.
The dependent variable was MCLS connectivity, and the independent variables were Group (SUD+ and SUD−), Site (South Bronx and San Juan), and a Group by Site interaction term.

Partial correlations between MCLS connectivity and impulsivity were calculated while controlling for site and group (SUD+ or SUD−), restricted to regions in which connectivity differed between SUD+ and SUD− participants.
The first linear regression model tested the association between impulsivity and low MCLS connectivity, defined as left NAcc − left OFC connection strength.
The second linear regression model tested whether MCLS connectivity predicted SUD while controlling for impulsivity.
The indirect effect of impulsivity on SUD as mediated by MCLS connectivity was tested using bias corrected bootstrapping.
Group differences in RMS and peak/average Framewise Displacement head motion parameters were tested.
